algo-01-c1.text: Ruth Anderson (University of Washington, CSE332) (2025). CSE332: Data Structures & Parallelism, Lecture 2: Algorithm Analysis. University of Washington, Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering.
algo-01-c1.quote: g(n) is in O( f(n) ) if there exist constants c and n0 such that g(n) ≤ c f(n) for all n ≥ n0
algo-01-c1.claim: Formally, f(n) = O(g(n)) means there exist constants c and n₀ such that f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n₀.

algo-01-c2.text: Stanford University CS 161 course staff (2018). Lecture 6: Sorting lower bounds and O(n)-time sorting. Stanford University, CS 161 Design and Analysis of Algorithms.
algo-01-c2.quote: Any deterministic comparison-based sorting algorithm must take Ω(n log(n)) steps.
algo-01-c2.claim: O(n log n) is the best a comparison sort can do.

algo-01-c3.text: Carnegie Mellon University 15-451/651 course staff (2022). Lecture #3: Amortized Analysis. Carnegie Mellon University, 15-451/651 Design & Analysis of Algorithms.
algo-01-c3.quote: The amortized cost (using the aggregate method) of append using the array-doubling algorithm is 3
algo-01-c3.claim: A single dynamic array append is usually O(1) but occasionally triggers an O(n) resize.

algo-02-c1.text: Robert Sedgewick, Kevin Wayne. Mergesort. Algorithms, 4th Edition (Princeton University).
algo-02-c1.quote: No compare-based sorting algorithm can guarantee to sort N items with fewer than lg(N!) ~ N lg N compares.
algo-02-c1.claim: There's a theoretical limit: any comparison sort takes at least Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case.

algo-02-c1.text: Robert Sedgewick, Kevin Wayne. Mergesort. Algorithms, 4th Edition (Princeton University).
algo-02-c1.quote: Mergesort is an asymptotically optimal compare-based sorting algorithm.
algo-02-c1.claim: Mergesort achieves the optimal O(n log n) in worst case.

algo-02-c2.text: Arrays (Java SE 21 & JDK 21). Oracle Java Documentation.
algo-02-c2.quote: The sorting algorithm is a Dual-Pivot Quicksort by Vladimir Yaroslavskiy, Jon Bentley, and Joshua Bloch.
algo-02-c2.claim: Timsort is what Python's sort() and Java's Arrays.sort for objects actually use (Java sorts primitive arrays with dual-pivot quicksort).

algo-02-c2.text: Andrew Dalke, Raymond Hettinger. Sorting Techniques. Python documentation.
algo-02-c2.quote: Sorts are guaranteed to be stable. That means that when multiple records have the same key, their original order is preserved.
algo-02-c2.claim: A sort is stable if equal elements keep their original order.

algo-03-c1.text: Robert Sedgewick, Kevin Wayne. Elementary Symbol Tables. Algorithms, 4th Edition (Princeton University).
algo-03-c1.quote: Proposition B. Binary search in an ordered array with N keys uses no more than lg N + 1 compares for a search (successful or unsuccessful) in the worst case.
algo-03-c1.claim: Binary search requires sorted input but achieves O(log n).

algo-03-c2.text: Robert Sedgewick, Kevin Wayne. Undirected Graphs. Algorithms, 4th Edition (Princeton University).
algo-03-c2.quote: To find a shortest path from s to v, we start at s and check for v among all the vertices that we can reach by following one edge, then we check for v among all the vertices that we can reach from s by following two edges, and so forth.
algo-03-c2.claim: Breadth-First Search (BFS) explores a graph layer by layer.

algo-03-c3.text: Robert Sedgewick, Kevin Wayne. Shortest Paths. Algorithms, 4th Edition (Princeton University).
algo-03-c3.quote: Dijkstra's algorithm solves the single-source shortest-paths problem in edge-weighted digraphs with nonnegative weights using extra space proportional to V and time proportional to E log V (in the worst case).
algo-03-c3.claim: With a binary heap, Dijkstra runs in O((V + E) log V).

algo-03-c3.text: Robert Sedgewick, Kevin Wayne. Shortest Paths. Algorithms, 4th Edition (Princeton University).
algo-03-c3.quote: The Bellman-Ford algorithm solves the single-source shortest-paths problem from a given source s (or finds a negative cycle reachable from s) for any edge-weighted digraph with V vertices and E edges, in time proportional to E V and extra space proportional to V, in the worst case.
algo-03-c3.claim: For those, use Bellman-Ford (O(VE), handles negative edges and detects negative cycles).

algo-04-c1.text: Alex Shinn, John Cowan, Arthur A. Gleckler (editors) (2013). Revised7 Report on the Algorithmic Language Scheme. Scheme Steering Committee (R7RS small).
algo-04-c1.quote: Implementations of Scheme are required to be properly tail-recursive. This allows the execution of an iterative computation in constant space, even if the iterative computation is described by a syntactically recursive procedure.
algo-04-c1.claim: Some languages (Scheme, OCaml, Scala) optimize tail recursion into loops, eliminating the stack cost; others (Python, Java) don't.

algo-04-c2.text: Robert Sedgewick, Kevin Wayne. Mergesort. Algorithms, 4th Edition (Princeton University).
algo-04-c2.quote: This operation immediately lends itself to a simple recursive sort method known as mergesort: to sort an array, divide it into two halves, sort the two halves (recursively), and then merge the results.
algo-04-c2.claim: Mergesort splits the array, sorts halves, merges.

algo-04-c3.text: Jeff Erickson (2019). Backtracking. Algorithms (open textbook, University of Illinois).
algo-04-c3.quote: A backtracking algorithm tries to construct a solution to a computational problem incrementally, one small piece at a time.
algo-04-c3.claim: The skeleton: try a partial solution; if it can extend to a complete one, recurse; otherwise undo ("backtrack") and try the next option.

algo-05-c1.text: Jeff Erickson (2019). Dynamic Programming. Algorithms (open textbook, University of Illinois).
algo-05-c1.quote: In a nutshell, dynamic programming is recursion without repetition. Dynamic programming algorithms store the solutions of intermediate subproblems, often but not always in some kind of array or table.
algo-05-c1.claim: When both hold, you can solve once, store, reuse, turning exponential brute force into polynomial.

algo-05-c2.text: Robert Sedgewick, Kevin Wayne. Minimum Spanning Trees. Algorithms, 4th Edition (Princeton University).
algo-05-c2.quote: The cut property is the basis for the algorithms that we consider for the MST problem. Specifically, they are special cases of the greedy algorithm.
algo-05-c2.claim: Kruskal's and Prim's algorithms for minimum spanning trees are greedy and optimal.

algo-05-c2.text: Jeff Erickson (2019). Greedy Algorithms. Algorithms (open textbook, University of Illinois).
algo-05-c2.quote: The basic structure of this correctness proof is exactly the same as for the tape-sorting problem: an inductive exchange argument.
algo-05-c2.claim: Recognizing when greedy is correct (and when it isn't) is the harder skill, proving optimality usually requires an exchange argument or matroid theory.

algo-05-c3.text: Jeff Erickson (2019). NP-Hardness. Algorithms (open textbook, University of Illinois).
algo-05-c3.quote: There are several so-called NP-hard problems, which most people believe cannot be solved in polynomial time, even though nobody can prove a super-polynomial lower bound.
algo-05-c3.claim: The traveling salesman problem (TSP), boolean satisfiability (SAT), graph coloring, knapsack (0/1 integer), and many others sit in NP-complete: solvable in polynomial time only if P = NP, which most researchers believe is false.
